definitions.definition: A rule of physics that says things naturally go from order to disorder over time.
definitions.example: An ice cube melts into a puddle because the water molecules spread out randomly.

definitions.definition: Something that stays the same even when other things change around it.
definitions.example: The number 2 is always 2, whether you're counting apples or planets.

definitions.definition: A Greek word meaning 'Word' or 'reason,' used in the Bible to describe God's eternal logic and order that created and holds everything together.
definitions.example: Like the blueprint that makes a building stable and functional.

definitions.definition: The idea that physical reality comes from information, not the other way around.
definitions.example: Think of a computer game where the graphics and rules are made from code, not from physical stuff.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; things tend to get more disordered over time.
definitions.example: A messy room gets messier on its own, but it takes work to clean it up.

definitions.definition: A rule that says every symmetry in nature leads to a conservation law, like energy being conserved.
definitions.example: If a snowflake is perfectly symmetrical, some property of it stays the same no matter how you rotate it.

definitions.definition: Rules that say certain things (like energy or mass) can't be created or destroyed, only changed form.
definitions.example: When you burn wood, the mass turns into ash and smoke, but the total amount of matter stays the same.

definitions.definition: The quality of not depending on anything else for existence; being necessary.
definitions.example: A rock exists because of other things, but a non-contingent thing would exist all by itself forever.

definitions.definition: Being true no matter what perspective or situation you look at it from.
definitions.example: The fact that 2+2=4 is true whether you're on Earth or on Mars.

definitions.definition: Not being able to be figured out or proven from simpler facts alone.
definitions.example: You can't prove that kindness is good just by looking at atoms and molecules.

definitions.definition: Being useful or true in many different areas of knowledge.
definitions.example: The idea of fairness applies to games, school, and jobs, not just one place.

definitions.definition: The opposite of entropy; a measure of order or organization that resists the natural trend toward disorder.
definitions.example: A living plant is negentropic because it takes energy from the sun to build complex structures.

definitions.definition: When parts of a system are connected and work together in a stable, orderly way.
definitions.example: A choir singing in harmony has coherence; random noise does not.

definitions.definition: The process where a system loses its orderly connections and becomes random or separate.
definitions.example: When a choir stops singing together and everyone hums a different tune, that's decoherence.

definitions.definition: A theory that all the information in a volume of space can be stored on its surface, like a hologram.
definitions.example: Imagine a 3D movie stored on a flat DVD; the flat surface holds all the 3D info.

definitions.definition: A state that tends to break down or change because it's not naturally balanced.
definitions.example: A sandcastle is thermodynamically unstable because waves will wash it away.

definitions.definition: The natural force that pushes things toward disorder over time.
definitions.example: The entropic pressure on a clean room makes it slowly get messy unless you clean it.

definitions.definition: The unchanging foundation or reality that everything else is based on.
definitions.example: Like the solid bedrock under a house that doesn't move even when the house shakes.

definitions.definition: How accurately a message is received compared to what was sent.
definitions.example: A clear phone call has high signal fidelity; a static-filled call has low fidelity.

definitions.definition: The medium or path through which information travels from sender to receiver.
definitions.example: A wire is a channel for electricity; the air is a channel for sound.

definitions.definition: Short for signal-to-noise ratio; how strong the true message is compared to random interference.
definitions.example: A high S/N means you can hear a friend clearly in a quiet room; low S/N means you can't hear them in a loud party.

definitions.definition: Default Mode Network; a set of brain regions active when you're daydreaming or thinking about yourself.
definitions.example: When you're not focused on a task, your DMN is active and you might think about memories or future plans.

definitions.definition: The basic foundation or reason why something exists or is real.
definitions.example: Saying 'gravity exists because of mass' is an ontological grounding for gravity.

definitions.definition: The exact opposite characteristics of something, especially of truth or goodness.
definitions.example: If truth is stable, the anti-property would be instability.
